content: The text provided is a long and complex compilation of references, study details, and search strategies related to infant and child feeding practices, nutritional outcomes, and health impacts. 1. Dhami MV, Ogbo FA, Diallo TMO, Agho KE conducted a regional analysis in 2020 to investigate the associations between infant and young child feeding practices and the prevalence of diarrhea among Indian children. The findings were published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2. Popkin BM, Adair L, Akin JS, Black R, Briscoe J, and Flieger W explored the relationship between breastfeeding and diarrheal morbidity in infants. Their study, published in Pediatrics in 1990, highlighted the protective effects of breastfeeding against diarrheal diseases. 3. Eaton-Evans J and Dugdale AE examined the effects of feeding methods and social factors on the incidence of diarrhea and vomiting in infants. Their findings, published in Archives of Disease in Childhood in 1987, emphasized the role of feeding practices in gastrointestinal health. 4. Kalanda BF, Verhoeff FH, and Brabin BJ studied breastfeeding and complementary feeding practices in Malawian infants, focusing on their impact on morbidity and growth. Their research, published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2006, provided insights into the nutritional and health outcomes of these practices. 5. Mondal SK, Gupta PG, Gupta DN, Ghosh S, Sikder SN, Rajendran K, et al. investigated the occurrence of diarrheal diseases in relation to infant feeding practices in a rural community in West Bengal, India. Their study, published in Acta Paediatrica in 1996, highlighted the importance of appropriate feeding practices in reducing diarrheal morbidity. 6. English LK, Obbagy JE, Wong YP, Butte NF, Dewey KG, Fox MK, et al. conducted a systematic review in 2019 to assess the timing of the introduction of complementary foods and beverages and its effects on growth, size, and body composition. The review was published in The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 7. Bainbridge (1996) conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) in Ohio, USA, involving healthy, full-term infants. The study compared the effects of cereal feeding versus formula feeding on various outcomes, including weight, length, skinfold thickness, and biochemical markers such as calcium and vitamin D levels. 8. Dewey (1998) conducted an RCT in Honduras involving healthy, full-term infants. The study compared breastfeeding practices and their effects on lactational amenorrhea, energy intake, weight gain, and morbidity. 9. Dewey (2004) conducted another RCT in Honduras, focusing on low-birth-weight (LBW) infants. The study assessed the impact of breastfeeding on hemoglobin levels, ferritin, vitamin A, and zinc levels, as well as growth and morbidity outcomes. 10. Gupta (2017) conducted an RCT in India involving preterm and small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants. The study compared complementary feeding at 4 months versus 6 months and evaluated outcomes such as weight-for-age z-scores, neurodevelopment, and dietary diversity. 11. Jonsdottir (2014) conducted an RCT in Iceland involving healthy, full-term infants. The study compared exclusive breastfeeding with complementary feeding and assessed developmental outcomes, growth parameters, and iron status. 12. Kattelmann (2001) conducted an RCT in Ohio, USA, involving healthy, full-term infants. The study compared early versus late introduction of commercial complementary foods and their effects on dietary intake, growth, and body composition. 13. Marriott (2003) conducted an RCT in the United Kingdom involving preterm infants. The study compared complementary feeding after 3 months versus 4 months and evaluated growth velocities, energy intake, and iron status. 14. Perkin (2018) conducted an RCT in the United Kingdom involving full-term infants. The study compared early introduction of complementary foods at 3 months versus standard introduction at 6 months and assessed outcomes such as sleep and allergy development. 15. Skjerven (2020) conducted an RCT in Norway and Sweden involving healthy infants. The study compared skin and food interventions with no intervention and assessed outcomes such as atopic dermatitis and hospitalization events. 16. Sloan (2007) conducted an ambi-directional cohort study in Northern Ireland involving full-term infants aged 10-14 months. The study assessed the impact of breastfeeding initiation and prelacteal feeding on weight gain. 17. Sreedhara (2014) conducted a retrospective cohort study in India involving full-term infants aged 9-12 months. The study evaluated the effects of breastfeeding duration on growth parameters and stunting. 18. Sun (2016) conducted a retrospective cohort study in Australia involving healthy, full-term infants aged 9-15 months. The study assessed the timing of complementary feeding and its impact on growth, BMI, and food preferences. 19. WHO Working Group (2002) conducted a prospective cohort study across multiple countries, including China, India, Africa, Chile, Sweden, and Australia. The study evaluated the impact of breastfeeding on growth velocity and attained height and weight. 20. Hua (2017) conducted a prospective cohort study in Taiwan involving full-term infants. The study assessed the timing of complementary feeding and its effects on immune markers such as serum IgE levels. 21. Hollis (2016) conducted a prospective cohort study in the United Kingdom involving full-term infants. The study evaluated the impact of breastfeeding duration on growth, BMI, and food preferences. 22. Heinig (1993) conducted a prospective cohort study in the United States involving full-term infants. The study assessed the effects of breastfeeding and formula feeding on growth and developmental milestones. 23. Vijayalakshmi (2015) conducted a retrospective cohort study involving infants aged 6-24 months. The study evaluated the impact of complementary feeding practices on growth and nutritional status. 24. Huh (2011) conducted a prospective cohort study in the United States involving healthy children. The study assessed the timing of complementary feeding and its effects on growth and BMI. 25. Eaton-Evans (1987) conducted a prospective cohort study in Australia involving full-term infants. The study evaluated the impact of solid food introduction on diarrhea and vomiting. 26. Barrera (2016) conducted a retrospective cohort study involving healthy, term infants. The study assessed the timing of complementary feeding and its effects on growth and obesity. 27. Carneiro (2015) conducted a retrospective cohort study in Brazil involving infants aged 4-8 months. The study evaluated growth curves for weight and height. 28. Abraham (2012) conducted an ambi-directional cohort study in the United Kingdom involving children aged 9-12 months. The study assessed breastfeeding practices and their impact on BMI and dietary patterns. 29. Asfaw (2015) conducted a retrospective cohort study in South Ethiopia involving children aged 6-59 months. The study evaluated the impact of breastfeeding and prelacteal feeding on growth and nutritional status. 30. Baker (2004) conducted a retrospective cohort study in Denmark involving healthy, full-term infants. The study assessed the impact of breastfeeding and formula feeding on growth at 1 year. 31. Caleyachetty (2013) conducted a retrospective cohort study in India involving infants. The study evaluated the impact of breastfeeding duration on growth and body composition. 32. Davies-Adetugbo (1997) conducted a prospective cohort study in Nigeria involving healthy term infants. The study assessed the impact of breastfeeding initiation on growth and nutritional status. 33. Grote (2011) conducted a prospective cohort study across multiple European countries involving healthy, singleton, term infants. The study evaluated the impact of formula feeding on growth and BMI. 34. Joseph (2011) conducted a prospective cohort study in the United States involving infants recruited at birth. The study assessed the impact of breastfeeding on food sensitization. 35. Johnson (2014) conducted a retrospective cohort study in England and Wales involving healthy, term infants. The study evaluated the impact of breastfeeding on weight gain and food fussiness. 36. Kalanda (2006) conducted a prospective cohort study in Malawi involving infants. The study assessed the impact of breastfeeding on growth, morbidity, and nutritional status. 37. Rossiter (2013) conducted a prospective cohort study in Canada involving healthy children. The study evaluated the impact of breastfeeding and formula feeding on growth and BMI. 38. Koplin (2010) conducted a prospective cohort study in Australia involving infants aged 11-15 months. The study assessed the impact of breastfeeding on egg allergy development. 39. Makela (2014) conducted a prospective cohort study in Finland involving healthy infants. The study evaluated the impact of breastfeeding on growth and BMI. 40. Lee (2020) conducted a retrospective cohort study in Korea involving healthy children aged 1-3 years. The study assessed the impact of breastfeeding and formula feeding on atopic dermatitis and asthma. 41. Luccioli (2014) conducted a retrospective cohort study in the United States involving healthy children. The study evaluated the impact of exclusive breastfeeding on food allergies. 42. Lin (2013) conducted a prospective cohort study in China involving full-term births. The study assessed the impact of breastfeeding on growth and BMI. 43. Mannan (2018) conducted a prospective cohort study in Australia involving healthy children. The study evaluated the impact of breastfeeding and complementary feeding on growth and nutritional outcomes.
